questions.q: Isn't an LLM judge faster than all this?
questions.a: Use it for one narrow job: saying whether the diff that followed a comment addressed it. Grading quality rewards how a comment reads, and judges have known biases. In Zheng et al. (2023), padding an answer with a repeated list fooled Claude-v1 and GPT-3.5 in 91.3% of tries (GPT-4 in 8.7%), and GPT-4 gave the same verdict with the answers swapped only 65% of the time. Spot-check its labels against people.

questions.q: The author changed the line. Did the comment cause it?
questions.a: Not necessarily: a test may have failed, or a colleague said the same. Compare with pull requests where the skill was off, or wrote comments without posting them, and credit it only with the difference.

teach.title: How it works: a feedback loop from real pull requests

questions.q: When would you delete the skill?
questions.a: When it doesn't beat no skill on acted-on comments per pull request in a fair live test. Anthropic's skill guide says to measure the agent without the skill first, and a loaded skill's tokens compete with the rest of the context, so a useless skill still costs every review.

teach.title: How it works: a feedback loop from real pull requests

questions.q: What is a change trigger in the Bosu et al. Microsoft study?
questions.a: A review comment followed, in a later version of the same pull request, by a code change within one line of the lines it pointed at. As a sign that the author found the comment useful, it had 88% precision and 78% recall.

teach.title: How it works: a feedback loop from real pull requests

questions.q: Why is “share of a review skill's comments acted on” easy to game?
questions.a: The skill decides how many comments to post. Posting fewer, safer comments raises the share while catching fewer problems. Count acted-on comments per pull request instead, and track missed bugs beside it.

questions.q: What does Google's Tricorder do with an analyzer that developers find noisy?
questions.a: It tracks the analyzer's not-useful rate from developers' clicks in code review. At 10% or more the analyzer goes on probation and its writer must show progress; above 25% it may be turned off. The fix can be as simple as rewording its messages.
